meta.author: Gareth Montgomery (GarethEnglish.com)
meta.privacyStandard: 100% anonymised classroom corpus (zero student names, portal slugs, cities, or employers)

categoryComparison.label: Tense, Aspect & Conditional Timing
categoryComparison.spokenMechanism: Real-time clause launch: speakers utter an auxiliary ("I have...", "If they would...") before selecting the finished past time anchor at the end of the breath group.
categoryComparison.writtenMechanism: Low incidence in untimed essays because writers visually scan back over finished time markers ("in 2022", "last week") before moving on.

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S02 · Slavic L1
sampleSpoken.spoken: Attackers have stolen over six hundred million dollars in March 2022.
sampleSpoken.repair: Attackers stole over six hundred million dollars in March 2022.
sampleSpoken.rule: Past Simple is mandatory when anchored to a finished past date ("in March 2022").

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S02 · Slavic L1
sampleSpoken.spoken: If the engineer would not open that PDF file, the network would stay safe.
sampleSpoken.repair: If the engineer had not opened that PDF file, the network would have stayed safe.
sampleSpoken.rule: Never put modal "would" inside the conditional if-clause; unreal past requires Past Perfect ("had not opened").

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S02 · Slavic L1
sampleSpoken.spoken: Lately, security teams saw a huge rise in voice-cloning scams.
sampleSpoken.repair: Lately, security teams have seen a sharp rise in voice-cloning scams.
sampleSpoken.rule: "Lately" connects recent events to the present window and requires Present Perfect ("have seen"), not Past Simple.

sampleWritten.detail: Future time clause with "will" ("when you will arrive" -> "when you arrive").
Past narrative drift inside timeless review summary ("The album starts quietly and then it suddenly shifted...").

categoryComparison.label: Preposition Calques & Verb Valency
categoryComparison.spokenMechanism: Direct L1 preposition and verb-complement transfer ("arrive to", "discuss about", "explain me", "depends of", "plans on next month") under live conversational speed.
categoryComparison.writtenMechanism: Persists in writing around dependent prepositions after abstract nouns and verbs, though overt spoken valency slips ("explain me") drop sharply.

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S01 · East Slavic L1
sampleSpoken.spoken: I have been living on Malta for three years.
sampleSpoken.repair: I have been living in Malta for three years.
sampleSpoken.rule: Use "in" for sovereign countries/states even when geographically an island ("on the island", "in Malta").

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S01 · East Slavic L1
sampleSpoken.spoken: I cannot tolerate when team members ignore safety checks.
sampleSpoken.repair: I cannot tolerate it when team members ignore safety checks.
sampleSpoken.rule: Transitive verbs of dislike ("tolerate / stand / bear / hate + it + when") require preparatory object "it" before a when-clause.

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S03 · Armenian/Russian L1
sampleSpoken.spoken: When visitors arrive to Lisbon in spring, the light is extraordinary.
sampleSpoken.repair: When visitors arrive in Lisbon in spring, the light is extraordinary.
sampleSpoken.rule: "Arrive" never takes "to": use "arrive in" (cities/countries) or "arrive at" (stations/buildings/events).

sampleWritten.detail: Preposition slip "access for historical collections" instead of "access to historical collections".
Dependent preposition slip "awareness to habitat loss" -> "awareness of habitat loss".

categoryComparison.label: Articles, Determiners & Countability
categoryComparison.spokenMechanism: Dropped indefinite articles before singular countable role/place nouns ("in open-plan office", "to senior engineer") and exclamative uncountables ("What a wonderful news!").
categoryComparison.writtenMechanism: Surges to the #1 error category in formal essays because academic prose packs abstract uncountable nouns ("staffs", "infrastructures", "researches", "damages") and generic plurals ("the society") into every clause.

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S02 · Slavic L1
sampleSpoken.spoken: They sent fake job offer to senior engineer on LinkedIn.
sampleSpoken.repair: They sent a fake job offer to a senior engineer on LinkedIn.
sampleSpoken.rule: Singular countable nouns ("offer", "engineer") require an article even when modified by an adjective.

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S02 · Slavic L1
sampleSpoken.spoken: He messaged our developer pretending to be legitimate venture capital fund.
sampleSpoken.repair: He messaged our developer pretending to be a legitimate venture capital fund.
sampleSpoken.rule: Singular countable noun phrase ("a legitimate venture capital fund") requires indefinite article "a".

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S04 · Ukrainian/German L2
sampleSpoken.spoken: What a wonderful news that you can visit us in May!
sampleSpoken.repair: What wonderful news that you can visit us in May!
sampleSpoken.rule: "News" is strictly uncountable in English: never use indefinite article "a" ("What wonderful news!").

sampleWritten.detail: Missing indefinite article before modified singular noun ("build digital archive" -> "build a digital archive").

categoryComparison.label: False Friends & Word-Family Confusables
categoryComparison.spokenMechanism: Cognate and near-twin retrieval slips ("job perspectives" vs "career prospects", "human" vs "humane", "actually" vs "currently", "sensible" vs "sensitive").
categoryComparison.writtenMechanism: Appears in formal essays as suffix/part-of-speech misselections ("culture institutions", "deceivable", "frequenters") or dictionary-list misfires.

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S01 · East Slavic L1
sampleSpoken.spoken: Every stray animal deserves human treatment.
sampleSpoken.repair: Every stray animal deserves humane treatment.
sampleSpoken.rule: Word-family pair: "human" = relating to people; "humane" = compassionate, causing minimal pain.

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S03 · Armenian/Russian L1
sampleSpoken.spoken: Many graduates move abroad because they want better job perspectives.
sampleSpoken.repair: Many graduates move abroad because they want better career prospects.
sampleSpoken.rule: Classic false friend: "perspectives" = viewpoints/angles; "prospects" = future opportunities/chances of success.

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S04 · Ukrainian/German L2
sampleSpoken.spoken: After the walk you can take a sit on the terrace and lay down on the lawn.
sampleSpoken.repair: After the walk you can take a seat on the terrace and lie down on the lawn.
sampleSpoken.rule: Noun "a seat" (vs verb "sit") and intransitive verb "lie down" (vs transitive "lay something down").

sampleWritten.detail: Noun adjunct "culture institutions" instead of attributive adjective "cultural institutions".
Archaic/unnatural dictionary noun "frequenters" instead of "visitors / patrons".

categoryComparison.label: Embedded Question Inversion & Clause Boundaries
categoryComparison.spokenMechanism: Retaining direct-question inversion inside indirect clauses ("explain how did they bypass...", "see how does the system handle...") while monitoring listeners live.
categoryComparison.writtenMechanism: Direct-question inversion virtually disappears on paper, replaced instead by punctuation/comma-splice boundary slips and compound-modifier orthography.

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S02 · Slavic L1
sampleSpoken.spoken: Can you explain me how did they bypass two-factor authentication?
sampleSpoken.repair: Can you explain to me how they bypassed two-factor authentication?
sampleSpoken.rule: Double spoken trap: "explain + to + person" valency AND statement word order ("how they bypassed") inside an embedded question.

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S04 · Ukrainian/German L2
sampleSpoken.spoken: Old industrial heritage is exactly for what our region is famous.
sampleSpoken.repair: Old industrial heritage is what our region is famous for.
sampleSpoken.rule: Natural spoken nominal relative clause keeps the preposition at the end ("what our region is famous for").

sampleSpoken.speaker: Speaker S05 · Kartvelian L1
sampleSpoken.spoken: What does make Earth so suitable for complex ecosystems?
sampleSpoken.repair: What makes Earth so suitable for complex ecosystems?
sampleSpoken.rule: When "What" is the grammatical subject of the question, do not insert unemphatic auxiliary "does" ("What makes...").

sampleWritten.detail: Comma splice joining two independent finite clauses across ", therefore,".
Punctuation boundary slip after fronted comparative ("Even worse many governments..." missing comma / fragment join).

patterns.originalSlip: When visitors arrive to Lisbon in spring, the light is extraordinary.
patterns.dodgedStudentExample: Next month I want to come to Madrid to visit my cousin.
patterns.whyDodgeFails: Grammatically fine, but swaps "arrive" for safe B1 "come to" — leaving the "arrive to" reflex untouched next time the speaker reaches for "arrive" live.
patterns.lockedPersonalExample: Whenever I arrive in Vienna by train, I walk straight from the station after I arrive at the main platform.

patterns.targetStructure: have/has + been + -ing (or repeated Present Perfect) + lately
patterns.originalSlip: I have bought a new car lately.
patterns.dodgedStudentExample: I bought a new laptop two weeks ago.
patterns.whyDodgeFails: Switches to Past Simple + "ago" instead of practising "lately" with an ongoing or repeated activity.
patterns.lockedPersonalExample: I have been cycling to the studio lately because the morning traffic has grown heavier lately.

patterns.targetStructure: explain to [person] + wh-word + Subject + Verb (no do/did)
patterns.originalSlip: Can you explain me how did they bypass two-factor authentication?
patterns.dodgedStudentExample: How did the attackers enter the server?
patterns.whyDodgeFails: Reverts to a direct question (where "did" inversion IS legal) instead of practising statement order inside an indirect clause.
patterns.lockedPersonalExample: Could you explain to our client how the backup service encrypts customer records?

patterns.originalSlip: Tomorrow we need to discuss about the supplier contract.
patterns.dodgedStudentExample: Tomorrow we will have a talk about the supplier contract.
patterns.whyDodgeFails: Substitutes the noun "a talk about" (where "about" IS used), reinforcing the exact preposition reflex that corrupts the verb "discuss"!
patterns.lockedPersonalExample: Tomorrow morning I need to discuss the Q4 hiring budget with our finance lead.

interactiveClinicDrills.rawSpoken: I have bought a new car lately, so driving to work is much easier.
interactiveClinicDrills.blueprint: Single finished event + recently (Past Simple)  OR  have/has been + -ing + lately (ongoing habit)
interactiveClinicDrills.modelRepair: I bought a new car recently, so driving to work is much easier. (OR: I have been driving a new car lately.)
interactiveClinicDrills.personalLockLabel: Write 1 personal sentence using "have/has been + -ing + lately" (do NOT dodge to "ago" or "yesterday"):
interactiveClinicDrills.personalModel: I have been reading twenty pages in English before breakfast lately.
interactiveClinicDrills.explanation: "Lately" covers a recent window stretching up to the present moment, so it pairs with repeated actions or ongoing habits ("have been driving"), never a one-off completed transaction ("bought ... recently").

interactiveClinicDrills.rawSpoken: When travellers arrive to Lisbon in early May, the coastal breeze is warm.
interactiveClinicDrills.blueprint: arrive + IN + [city / country]   |   arrive + AT + [station / airport / building / event]
interactiveClinicDrills.modelRepair: When travellers arrive in Lisbon in early May, the coastal breeze is warm.
interactiveClinicDrills.personalLockLabel: Write 1 personal sentence using "arrive in" or "arrive at" (do NOT dodge to "come to" or "go to"):
interactiveClinicDrills.personalModel: Whenever I arrive at the airport early, I grab a black coffee before boarding.
interactiveClinicDrills.explanation: Movement verbs "go to / get to / come to" pull speakers into saying "arrive to". English treats "arrive" as reaching a boundary, never travelling toward one: "arrive in" (city/country) or "arrive at" (venue).

interactiveClinicDrills.rawSpoken: Can you explain me how did they bypass two-factor authentication?
interactiveClinicDrills.slipHighlight: explain me how did they bypass
interactiveClinicDrills.blueprint: explain + TO [person] + wh-word + Subject + Verb (statement order — drop do/does/did)
interactiveClinicDrills.modelRepair: Can you explain to me how they bypassed two-factor authentication?
interactiveClinicDrills.personalLockLabel: Write 1 sentence using "explain to [person] how/why + Subject + Verb" (no "did/do/does" inversion!):
interactiveClinicDrills.personalModel: I had to explain to my manager why the migration took an extra afternoon.
interactiveClinicDrills.explanation: Two classic spoken retrieval slips in six words: "explain" always needs "to" before the listener ("explain to me"), and once "Can you..." carries the question inversion, the second clause reverts to calm statement order ("how they bypassed").

interactiveClinicDrills.rawSpoken: If engineering managers would reduce daily status calls, teams would finish much earlier.
interactiveClinicDrills.blueprint: If + Subject + Past Simple [unreal present], Subject + would + bare infinitive
interactiveClinicDrills.modelRepair: If engineering managers reduced daily status calls, teams would finish much earlier.
interactiveClinicDrills.personalLockLabel: Write 1 hypothetical sentence starting with "If [Subject] + Past Simple, ... would ..." (zero "would" in the if-clause!):
interactiveClinicDrills.personalModel: If public transport ran every ten minutes at night, fewer residents would drive into town.
interactiveClinicDrills.explanation: In live speech across Slavic, German, and Romance L1s, speakers mirror the subjunctive modal in both halves ("If X would..., Y would..."). Keep "would" strictly in the result clause and lock the if-clause into Past Simple ("reduced").

interactiveClinicDrills.rawSpoken: In tomorrow’s meeting we need to discuss about the supplier contract.
interactiveClinicDrills.blueprint: discuss + [Direct Object] (ZERO preposition)   [Compare noun: a discussion about X]
interactiveClinicDrills.modelRepair: In tomorrow’s meeting we need to discuss the supplier contract.
interactiveClinicDrills.personalLockLabel: Write 1 sentence with the verb "discuss + [Direct Object]" (do NOT dodge to "talk about" or "a discussion about"):
interactiveClinicDrills.personalModel: On Friday afternoon I will discuss our quarterly targets with the regional lead.
interactiveClinicDrills.explanation: Every week in business English sessions, senior directors say "discuss about" because "talk about" and "a discussion about" sit right beside it in memory. Drill the bare verb + object collision ("discuss the contract") out loud.

interactiveClinicDrills.rawSpoken: Actually, I see fourteen private clients a week, though last year I saw twenty.
interactiveClinicDrills.blueprint: Currently / At the moment [= right now]   ≠   Actually [= in fact / correcting a misconception]
interactiveClinicDrills.modelRepair: Currently, I see fourteen private clients a week, though last year I saw twenty.
interactiveClinicDrills.personalLockLabel: Write 1 sentence starting with "Currently," to describe your present work or study routine:
interactiveClinicDrills.personalModel: Currently, I prepare two Cambridge C1 classes and three IELTS tutorials each Tuesday.
interactiveClinicDrills.explanation: European cognates ("actualmente / actuellement / aktuell / aktualnie") all mean "right now". When you start an English answer with "Actually,", listeners think you are politely contradicting them!

interactiveClinicDrills.rawSpoken: What a wonderful news that your sister passed her medical finals!
interactiveClinicDrills.blueprint: What + Adjective + [Uncountable Noun]! (ZERO "a/an" with news, advice, weather, progress)
interactiveClinicDrills.modelRepair: What wonderful news that your sister passed her medical finals!
interactiveClinicDrills.personalLockLabel: Write 1 exclamation with "What + adjective + news / advice / weather / progress!" (no "a/an"!):
interactiveClinicDrills.personalModel: What encouraging progress you have made on your Part 3 timing this month!
interactiveClinicDrills.explanation: Because "What a..." is drilled as a fixed chunk ("What a great idea!"), speakers blurt out "What a..." before realising the noun at the end ("news", "weather", "advice") is uncountable.

interactiveClinicDrills.rawSpoken: I am working on distributed storage systems since 2023.
interactiveClinicDrills.blueprint: Subject + have/has + been + -ing + since [starting point] / for [duration]
interactiveClinicDrills.modelRepair: I have been working on distributed storage systems since 2023.
interactiveClinicDrills.personalLockLabel: Write 1 personal sentence using "I have been + -ing ... since [year/month]" or "... for [duration]":
interactiveClinicDrills.personalModel: I have been teaching Cambridge and IELTS candidates for nineteen years.
interactiveClinicDrills.explanation: Most European languages use the normal Present tense ("I work / I am working here since 2023") to bridge past-to-present duration. English insists on Present Perfect ("have been working") the moment "since" or duration "for" enters the sentence.

classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.speaker: Speaker S01 · East Slavic L1
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.spoken: Our connecting flight was cancelled, so I was stuck at the airport overnight.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.repair: Our connecting flight was cancelled, leaving me stranded at the airport overnight.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.rule: 100% grammatical original; upgraded with resultative participle + C1 adjective "stranded".

classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.speaker: Speaker S01 · East Slavic L1
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.spoken: I got interested in local folklore and read several archival studies; some of them were fascinating.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.repair: I became intrigued by local folklore and read several archival studies, some of which were fascinating.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.rule: 100% grammatical original; upgraded with C1 partitive relative clause (", some of which...").

classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.speaker: Speaker S01 · East Slavic L1
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.spoken: The benchmark figures for the new release were a bit disappointing.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.repair: The benchmark figures for the new release were rather underwhelming.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.rule: 100% grammatical original; upgraded to measured British evaluative register ("rather underwhelming").

classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.speaker: Speaker S01 · East Slavic L1
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.spoken: It put the regional office in a difficult situation with no easy solution.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.repair: It left the regional office in a difficult predicament.

classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.speaker: Speaker S01 · East Slavic L1
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.spoken: In everyday speech, people call that district the old harbour.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.repair: Colloquially, people refer to that district as the old harbour.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.rule: 100% grammatical original; upgraded for C1/C2 speaking register.

classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.speaker: Speaker S02 · Slavic L1
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.spoken: They routed the funds through forty wallets so investigators could not trace them.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.repair: They routed the funds through forty wallets to cover their tracks.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.rule: 100% grammatical original; C1 idiomatic upgrade ("cover their tracks").

classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.speaker: Speaker S02 · Slavic L1
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.spoken: The warning alert was missed by the night-shift team during the handover.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.repair: The warning alert slipped through the cracks during the handover.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.rule: 100% grammatical original; natural C1 phrasal idiom.

classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.speaker: Speaker S02 · Slavic L1
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.spoken: Nobody noticed the breach until a customer tried to withdraw funds.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.repair: It was not until a customer tried to withdraw funds that anyone noticed the breach.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.rule: 100% grammatical original; C1 "It was not until ... that ..." cleft upgrade.

classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.speaker: Speaker S02 · Slavic L1
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.spoken: Although the firm spent millions on firewalls, one phishing link compromised the server.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.repair: For all their investment in firewalls, a single phishing link compromised the server.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.rule: 100% grammatical original; C1 concessive frame ("For all + possessive + noun").

classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.speaker: Speaker S03 · Armenian/Russian L1
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.spoken: I really love the stripped-back acoustic arrangement on the final track.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.repair: What I really love about the final track is its stripped-back acoustic arrangement.
classroomStyleUpgradeExamples.rule: 100% grammatical original; C1 Wh-cleft focus upgrade for speaking & reviews.

essayEfsrCaseStudies.label: Case Study A · IELTS Task 2 (Global Biodiversity Loss)
essayEfsrCaseStudies.examTarget: IELTS Academic Writing Task 2 (Band 7.0 Baseline Confirmed)

styleFlagExamples.original: Scientists and policymakers have long discussed if human industrial activity is the primary driver of extinction.
styleFlagExamples.styleUpgrade: Scientists and policymakers have long debated whether human industrial activity is the primary driver of extinction.
styleFlagExamples.verdict: Style, not an error: "discussed if" is grammatical in standard English; "debated whether" is simply tighter formal register.

styleFlagExamples.original: Today, most of the living species in tropical reefs face rising ocean temperatures.
styleFlagExamples.styleUpgrade: Today, most living species in tropical reefs face rising ocean temperatures.
styleFlagExamples.verdict: Style, not an error: "most of the + plural noun" is grammatical when referring to a bounded set, though "most + plural noun" is cleaner for general reference.

styleFlagExamples.original: If conservation treaties fail, most of the species at the top of the food chain will vanish within decades.
styleFlagExamples.styleUpgrade: If conservation treaties fail, most species at the top of the food chain will vanish within decades.
styleFlagExamples.verdict: Style, not an error: completely grammatical clause; counting it as a grammar error penalises natural learner phrasing.

styleFlagExamples.original: So far, there has not been a clear international framework established to halt illegal logging.
styleFlagExamples.styleUpgrade: So far, no clear international framework has been established to halt illegal logging.
styleFlagExamples.verdict: Style, not an error: existential "there has not been ... established" is grammatical; active negative subject is merely more concise.

essayEfsrCaseStudies.label: Case Study B · C1 Advanced Proposal (Suburban Commuter Transport)

styleFlagExamples.original: Morning congestion continues to pose a serious challenge to commuters travelling from outer districts.
styleFlagExamples.styleUpgrade: Morning congestion continues to pose a serious challenge for commuters travelling from outer districts.
styleFlagExamples.verdict: Style, not an error: both "pose a challenge to" and "pose a challenge for" are attested in British academic & Cambridge corpus usage.

styleFlagExamples.original: It is strongly recommended that dedicated bus lanes be widened along the northern ring road.
styleFlagExamples.styleUpgrade: (Leave unchanged — Automated checker false positive on passive voice!)
styleFlagExamples.verdict: Style, not an error: automated writing tools flag passive voice as "weak", yet impersonal passive recommendations earn C1 register credit.

styleFlagExamples.original: People who live in outer suburbs currently spend nearly ninety minutes each day in stationary traffic.
styleFlagExamples.styleUpgrade: Outer-suburb residents currently spend nearly ninety minutes each day in stationary traffic.
styleFlagExamples.verdict: Style, not an error: defining relative clause "People who live in..." is 100% grammatical.

styleFlagExamples.original: Reliable rail links remain a very important factor in persuading drivers to leave their cars at home.
styleFlagExamples.styleUpgrade: Reliable rail links remain a decisive factor in persuading drivers to leave their cars at home.
styleFlagExamples.verdict: Style, not an error: "very important" is plain B2/C1 vocabulary, never a grammatical error — and far better than forced thesaurus words like "paramount".

essayEfsrCaseStudies.label: Case Study C · IELTS Task 2 (Public Cultural Funding)

styleFlagExamples.original: It is widely argued that public museums play a very important role in civic education.
styleFlagExamples.styleUpgrade: It is widely argued that public museums play a vital role in civic education.
styleFlagExamples.verdict: Style, not an error: automated checkers flag both the preparatory passive ("It is widely argued") and "very important", attacking a 100% clean C1 topic sentence!

redPenChallengeItems.sentence: Environmental economists have long discussed if carbon taxes penalise rural households unfairly.
redPenChallengeItems.automatedCheckerReaction: Often underlined in amber/red ("Use whether instead of if" / "Wordy verb").
redPenChallengeItems.c1Upgrade: Environmental economists have long debated whether carbon taxes penalise rural households unfairly.
redPenChallengeItems.ruleFormula: discuss + if/whether + clause (grammatical)  →  debate + whether + clause (C1 register upgrade)
redPenChallengeItems.explanation: In British and Cambridge standard English, "discuss if/whether" is grammatical. Upgrading to "debated whether" sharpens academic tone, but red-penning the original as a grammar error is wrong and unfairly lowers EFSR.

redPenChallengeItems.sentence: Unregulated trawling has caused countless damages to fragile seabed ecosystems.
redPenChallengeItems.automatedCheckerReaction: Frequently MISSED by automated checkers because plural "damages" is a valid legal spelling!
redPenChallengeItems.c1Upgrade: Unregulated trawling has caused widespread damage to fragile seabed ecosystems.
redPenChallengeItems.ruleFormula: damage [uncountable = physical harm]  ≠  damages [plural legal = financial compensation]
redPenChallengeItems.explanation: Physical or environmental harm is strictly uncountable ("damage", never "damages" or "a damage"). Plural "damages" means court-awarded money, so automated spell-checkers sail right past it while human examiners penalise it immediately.

redPenChallengeItems.sentence: Without stricter marine reserves, most of the species in shallow coral reefs could vanish by 2060.
redPenChallengeItems.automatedCheckerReaction: Flagged as "wordy determiner — remove of the".
redPenChallengeItems.c1Upgrade: Without stricter marine reserves, most species in shallow coral reefs could vanish by 2060.
redPenChallengeItems.ruleFormula: most + plural noun [general]  /  most of the + plural noun + post-modifier [bounded set — grammatical!]
redPenChallengeItems.explanation: Because "species" is restricted here by "in shallow coral reefs", "most of the species in..." refers to a specific bounded group and is completely grammatical. Trimming to "most species" is a neat edit, not an error fix.

redPenChallengeItems.sentence: In my view, municipal councils should discuss about affordable housing before approving luxury towers.
redPenChallengeItems.automatedCheckerReaction: Usually caught, though learners often dodge it by writing "have a talk about".
redPenChallengeItems.c1Upgrade: In my view, municipal councils should discuss affordable housing before approving luxury towers.
redPenChallengeItems.ruleFormula: discuss + [Direct Object] (ZERO preposition)  vs.  a discussion + about + [Noun]
redPenChallengeItems.explanation: Verb "discuss" is directly transitive in English and never takes "about". Learners confuse the verb with the noun phrase "have a discussion about".

redPenChallengeItems.sentence: Ageing water pipes pose a serious challenge to regional authorities across northern Europe.
redPenChallengeItems.automatedCheckerReaction: Sometimes flagged by rigid style checkers demanding "pose a challenge for".
redPenChallengeItems.c1Upgrade: Ageing water pipes pose a serious challenge to (or for) regional authorities across northern Europe.
redPenChallengeItems.ruleFormula: pose a challenge + to / for + [Noun Phrase] (both idiomatic C1 collocations)
redPenChallengeItems.explanation: Both "pose a challenge to" and "pose a challenge for" are standard, high-scoring C1 collocations across Cambridge and academic corpora. Marking either preposition wrong is pure pedantry.

redPenChallengeItems.sentence: If national governments would invest earlier in grid storage, energy bills would be far lower today.
redPenChallengeItems.automatedCheckerReaction: Caught intermittently; often miscorrected into Present Simple instead of Mixed Conditional.
redPenChallengeItems.c1Upgrade: If national governments had invested earlier in grid storage, energy bills would be far lower today.
redPenChallengeItems.ruleFormula: If + Subject + had + V3 [unreal past], Subject + would + bare infinitive + today [present result]
redPenChallengeItems.explanation: Standard conditional clauses forbid "would" inside the if-branch. Because "earlier" refers to an unreal past failure with a result "today", this requires a mixed conditional ("had invested ... would be").

redPenChallengeItems.sentence: It is widely argued that free museum admission plays a very important role in civic education.
redPenChallengeItems.highlightSpan: It is widely argued ... very important
redPenChallengeItems.automatedCheckerReaction: Double false alarm: flags passive voice ("It is widely argued") AND flags "very important" as weak!
redPenChallengeItems.c1Upgrade: It is widely argued that free museum admission plays a vital role in civic education.
redPenChallengeItems.ruleFormula: It + BE + adverb + V3 + that + clause [C1 Preparatory Passive Reporting Frame]
redPenChallengeItems.explanation: Automated checkers routinely tell exam candidates to delete passive reporting frames ("It is widely argued that...") and swap plain "very important" for bloated thesaurus words ("paramount"). In reality, the passive frame earns C1 Grammatical Range credit and the sentence is 100% error-free.

redPenChallengeItems.sentence: Many university graduates relocate abroad because domestic firms offer limited job perspectives.
redPenChallengeItems.automatedCheckerReaction: Almost ALWAYS MISSED by automated grammar checkers because "job perspectives" is syntactically well-formed!
redPenChallengeItems.c1Upgrade: Many university graduates relocate abroad because domestic firms offer limited career prospects.
redPenChallengeItems.ruleFormula: career / job prospects [future opportunities]  ≠  perspectives [mental viewpoints / angles]
redPenChallengeItems.explanation: Across Slavic, German, and Romance languages, Cognate "perspektiva / perspective" means future career opportunities. In English, "perspectives" only means viewpoints; future opportunities are "prospects". Automated grammar checkers miss this completely.

redPenChallengeItems.sentence: To genuinely understand why rural clinics close, ministries must examine staff housing costs.
redPenChallengeItems.c1Upgrade: To understand genuinely (or To genuinely understand) why rural clinics close, ministries must examine staff housing costs.
redPenChallengeItems.ruleFormula: to + [single focusing adverb] + infinitive (fully accepted in modern British & Cambridge English)
redPenChallengeItems.explanation: The nineteenth-century Latinate ban on splitting an infinitive has never been an error in Cambridge or IELTS marking. Moving "genuinely" is optional rhythm, never a grammar mistake.

redPenChallengeItems.sentence: Public libraries depend of municipal grants to keep evening study rooms open.
redPenChallengeItems.c1Upgrade: Public libraries depend on municipal grants to keep evening study rooms open.
redPenChallengeItems.explanation: Direct Romance calque ("depender de / dipendere da"). In English, "depend" locks strictly onto "on" or "upon".

redPenChallengeItems.sentence: People who commute from outer towns spend nearly two hours a day on overcrowded trains.
redPenChallengeItems.highlightSpan: People who commute from outer towns
redPenChallengeItems.automatedCheckerReaction: AI rewriters highlight the whole subject and push unnatural nominal bloat ("Outer-municipality commuter cohorts").
redPenChallengeItems.c1Upgrade: Commuters from outer towns spend nearly two hours a day on overcrowded trains.
redPenChallengeItems.ruleFormula: Defining relative clause ("People who commute...") = 100% clean, natural English
redPenChallengeItems.explanation: There is nothing wrong with a clear defining relative clause. Compressing it to "Commuters from outer towns" saves two words, whereas AI rewriters often ruin natural voice with robotic jargon.

redPenChallengeItems.sentence: Recent neurological researches suggest that chronic sleep debt impairs memory consolidation.
redPenChallengeItems.automatedCheckerReaction: Sometimes missed because "researches" exists as a third-person singular verb ("she researches")!
redPenChallengeItems.c1Upgrade: Recent neurological research suggests (or Recent neurological studies suggest) that chronic sleep debt impairs memory consolidation.
redPenChallengeItems.ruleFormula: research / evidence / information / equipment [strictly uncountable]  →  use "studies" for plural
redPenChallengeItems.explanation: As a noun in modern exam and academic English, "research" is uncountable ("Recent research suggests..."). If you need a plural countable noun, use "studies" or "investigations".
